clue.text: Spooner’s assigned money for rock album

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so his version of a phrase trades its initial consonants

blocks.note: assigned means set; it takes the P sound from the next word in the swap
British money is counted in pounds; it takes the S sound from the previous word

explanation.surface: Someone muses about the budget set aside to buy a classic rock record.
explanation.walkthrough: SET POUNDS, said with the first sounds exchanged, becomes PET SOUNDS.
explanation.definitionFit: Pet Sounds is the celebrated 1966 studio record by the Beach Boys, an example of a pop-rock LP.

clue.text: Father involved in fast for period of bishop’s ruling

indicators.note: to be involved in something is to be caught up inside it, so one part sits within the other

blocks.note: PA is an informal word for one's dad

explanation.surface: A priest observes a fast during the time a bishop holds office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast' looks like going without food, but it means quick here. The bishop is the Bishop of Rome, the Pope.
explanation.definitionFit: The papacy is the term of office of a pope, who is himself Bishop of Rome.

clue.text: Woman rested with us after cycling

indicators.note: going round in a cycle brings letters from the front around to the back

blocks.note: past tense of sit, to take a rest
where we are, so 'us' points to this place

explanation.surface: A woman took a break with us after a bike ride.
explanation.walkthrough: SAT HERE is rotated so its opening SA moves to the end, giving THERESA. 'Cycling' sounds like riding a bicycle but means rotating the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Theresa is a female given name, and crosswords routinely clue any girl's name by woman.

clue.text: Remark with mail where watch is located

explanation.surface: A comment in a letter tells where a wristwatch has been found.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Watch' looks like a timepiece, but it is the act of keeping lookout.
explanation.definitionFit: A military lookout position from which sentries keep watch over enemy movements is called by this name.

clue.text: Extreme caution a director displays

indicators.note: to display is to put on show, so the words exhibit the answer already sitting in them

blocks.note: the run of letters spanning the end of the first word and start of the third

explanation.surface: A director shows extraordinary carefulness on set.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits across cautioN A DIRector.
explanation.definitionFit: A nadir is the lowest possible point, the bottom extremity of something's fortunes or a sky position.

clue.text: Barking “I couldn’t care less”, ignoring funny caller’s charm

indicators.note: barking means mad in British slang, so the letters go crazy and end up rearranged
to ignore something is to leave it out of account, so those letters are dropped
funny means odd or peculiar, so the letters to be removed appear scrambled rather than in order

blocks.note: the quoted phrase taken letter by letter
these letters, in any order, are removed from the phrase

explanation.surface: A nutty caller trying to woo someone shouts that they couldn't care less.
explanation.walkthrough: Strike the letters of CALLERS from I COULDN'T CARE LESS, leaving IOUDNTCES, then rearrange. 'Funny' tells you the removed letters are not in a block.
explanation.definitionFit: Seduction is the art of enticing or winning someone over, which is a sense of charm used as a noun.

clue.text: Clapped-out station wagon would normally be so

definitions.text: station wagon would normally be so

blocks.clueFragment: station wagon would normally be so
blocks.note: second meaning: a car normally has tyres fitted, a pun on the British spelling tyre

explanation.surface: An old estate car, which is usually fitted with wheels, has finally given up.
explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning plays on 'tyred', fitted with tyres (British spelling of tires), which is said the same way. A station wagon is a British estate car.
explanation.definitionFit: Something clapped-out is worn and exhausted, the everyday sense of weary; a vehicle on wheels is punningly 'tyred'.

clue.text: Greeting chief frequently heard lamenting past ambassador

indicators.note: what is heard is taken by ear, so the word counts by its sound not its spelling
past means beyond or after, so the grieving word is placed beyond the title word

blocks.note: oft is an old word for often
His Excellency, the title of an ambassador

explanation.surface: A senior figure keeps greeting people while grieving over a former diplomat.
explanation.walkthrough: HE is the abbreviation for His Excellency, used for ambassadors; 'past' places the grief word after him.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a cheery, traditionally Irish way to say hello early in the day.

clue.text: Decide turn with South taking over from first victor

indicators.note: taking over from someone means replacing them, and first says the earliest occurrence is the one swapped out

blocks.note: V is Victor in the radio alphabet

explanation.surface: A team decides its next move after the South side takes over from the earlier winner.
explanation.walkthrough: In REVOLVE the first V is replaced by S.
explanation.definitionFit: To resolve is to make up your mind firmly, a close synonym of determining a course.

clue.text: Obnoxious journos taking opposing views about trial

indicators.note: to take something is to hold it, so the outer pieces hold another between them
people with opposing views face opposite directions, so one of the pair is turned round

explanation.surface: Unpleasant reporters argue both sides of a court case.
explanation.walkthrough: The two EDs face opposite ways, one turned round, with the test between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Something obnoxious is loathed or hated, so detested here is an adjective describing the hated thing.

clue.text: Happy and relaxed by pool on vacation

indicators.note: vacation literally means emptying out, so the word keeps only its outer shell with the middle vacated

blocks.note: the word with its middle emptied

explanation.surface: A holidaymaker is content and at ease beside the swimming pool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On vacation' looks like a holiday but means emptied of contents. 'By' just places the pieces side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: Being pleased means feeling satisfied or content, a straightforward synonym of glad.

clue.text: Regularly visited Dieppe on ship to place

indicators.note: calling at regular intervals means stopping at every other spot, so only alternate letters are kept

blocks.note: first, third, fifth letters and so on

explanation.surface: A traveller regularly took the ferry to the French port of Dieppe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Visited' joins 'Regularly' as the instruction, so only every other letter is called on. 'To' is part of the fodder, not a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To deposit something is to put or set it down somewhere, a verb synonym of laying.

clue.text: Full chopper evacuating core from naval base

indicators.note: evacuating means emptying people out of a place, so these letters are removed from the word
the core of anything is its centre, so only the middle letter is wanted

blocks.note: e is the base of natural logarithms

explanation.surface: A packed helicopter airlifts people out of a military harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chopper' and 'evacuating' paint a helicopter rescue; in fact the chopper is a knife. Remove V and E from CLEAVER.
explanation.definitionFit: Clear can mean complete or entire, as in three clear days' notice, which matches full.

clue.text: Staggers around following everyone and drops from cliff

indicators.note: around means on every side of, so one piece is wrapped about the others

blocks.note: F is the abbreviation for following

explanation.surface: A drunk lurches about behind the crowd and falls off a cliff edge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drops' looks like a verb but is a plural noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Rockfalls are masses of stone tumbling down, descents of boulders from a crag or slope.

clue.text: Dish from America she once cooked

indicators.note: cooking transforms ingredients, and cooked books are falsified, so the letters are mixed into something new

explanation.surface: A woman once made a meal that came over from the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooked' fits the kitchen scene perfectly while telling you to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: This baked pasta in a sauce of melted cheddar is a familiar comfort food served as a meal.

clue.text: Protestant Oscar called celebrity up

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: Oscar is O in the radio alphabet
a big name is a famous person

explanation.surface: A Protestant phones a famous person.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'up' turns the celebrity word backwards. 'Oscar' looks like the film award but is just the letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: An Orangeman belongs to the Orange Order, a Protestant fraternal society in Northern Ireland.

clue.text: Sit-ins can be organised with such recognition for social distance

indicators.note: organising things puts them into a new arrangement, so the combined letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the phrase taken letter by letter
these letters are part of the mix that makes the phrase

explanation.surface: Protest sit-ins can be run in a way that wins praise for keeping people apart.
explanation.walkthrough: A compound anagram: SIT-INS plus the answer can be rearranged into SOCIAL DISTANCE, so take SIT-INS out of SOCIAL DISTANCE and rearrange what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: An accolade is an award or honour granted as praise, originally the ceremonial touch conferring knighthood.

clue.text: Maybe one church dignitary dead on back

indicators.note: going back means travelling the other way, so the short word is read in reverse

explanation.surface: A senior cleric may be lying dead on his back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe one' is the definition by example, not a stray phrase. 'Dead' means without feeling, not deceased.
explanation.definitionFit: One is an example of a counting value, the kind used for quantity rather than order, as opposed to ordinal.

clue.text: Once more register tenant accepting lease finally

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so one word receives a letter inside it
finally means at the very end, so just the closing letter of the word is used

explanation.surface: A tenant signs on again after finally agreeing to the lease.
explanation.walkthrough: The final letter of 'lease' goes inside the word for tenant, just after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To enter a record or name again is to log it a second time in a book or system.

clue.text: Use up each Spanish red

blocks.note: vino tinto is Spanish for red wine

explanation.surface: Someone finishes off a bottle each of Spanish red wine.
explanation.walkthrough: The Spanish word for red wine is tinto.
explanation.definitionFit: To eat into savings or time is to consume a portion of it, gradually depleting the supply.

clue.text: Keep back, hidden in auditorium

indicators.note: an auditorium is a hall built for listening, so the word is taken by its sound to an audience

explanation.surface: Someone stays out of sight at the back of a theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hidden' looks like a hidden-word signal, but it is the fragment that is said out loud; an auditorium is where audiences listen.
explanation.definitionFit: To hold up something is to delay or detain it, which is the sense of restraining progress.

clue.text: Public gathering poet’s near during hours of darkness

indicators.note: to gather something in is to collect and enclose it, so one piece takes the other inside

blocks.note: nigh is an old poetic word for near

explanation.surface: People assemble in public to hear verse read late into the evening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Public gathering' reads as a meeting, but 'gathering' means taking in.
explanation.definitionFit: Overnight describes something lasting through the night, the period after dark until morning.

clue.text: Projected broadcast from beginning to end

indicators.note: a broadcast goes out over the airwaves to listeners, so the word counts by how it sounds

blocks.note: through means all the way from start to finish

explanation.surface: A programme was shown on air in full from start to finish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Projected' looks like screening a film, but it means hurled.
explanation.definitionFit: To project something can mean to hurl it forward, so the past tense matches tossed or flung.

clue.text: Old-style railway system runs for miles

indicators.note: one thing for another means one in place of the other, so a letter is swapped

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned train network has services covering long distances.
explanation.walkthrough: Replace the M of METRO with R. 'Runs for miles' sounds like long journeys.
explanation.definitionFit: Retro describes a look or design that imitates fashions from an earlier era.

clue.text: Perhaps sonnet right to be included in advanced class

indicators.note: being included in a group means being put inside it, so one piece is placed within the other

blocks.note: A for advanced, as in A level
a form is a school class in Britain

explanation.surface: A teacher thinks a sonnet is fit for study by an upper school class.
explanation.walkthrough: The abbreviation for right goes between A and FORM, a British school year group.
explanation.definitionFit: A sonnet is one example of an established genre of creative work, here poetry with fixed structure.

clue.text: Was monarch restrained in conversation?

indicators.note: conversation is spoken talk, so the word is judged by its sound rather than its spelling

explanation.surface: It asks whether a king kept quiet while talking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Restrained in conversation' reads as being reticent, but the conversation is the signal to say the word aloud.
explanation.definitionFit: To have reigned is to have ruled as king or queen, so the past tense covers occupying a throne.

clue.text: Bird rues having clipped wings

indicators.note: a word's wings are its outer edges, and clipping trims them, so the first and last letters are cut

blocks.note: regrets is a verb meaning rues

explanation.surface: A bird is sorry that its wings have been trimmed.
explanation.walkthrough: Wings are the outer edges of a word, so both ends of REGRETS go.
explanation.definitionFit: An egret is a white wading heron with long legs, a specific kind of feathered creature.

clue.text: Eccentric purges own internet forum

indicators.note: eccentric means off-centre and unconventional, so the letters stray from their usual order

explanation.surface: An oddball deletes their own posts from an online discussion board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eccentric' looks like a person in the scene but is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A newsgroup is a Usenet discussion area where users post messages on a shared topic.
